summary: An excerpt from Kate Douglas Wiggin's Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm (labeled 'Book 11 — part 80') set in a village congregation. Mr. Burch, a missionary for a church building fund, has finished the final hymn and asks whether any sister will host him and his wife for a parlor meeting. The room falls silent because each householder has an excuse. Mrs. Robinson hints that the missionaries always stayed at the brick house, and Rebecca seizes the chance to offer the Sawyer aunts' hospitality, which impresses the congregation. Mr. Burch accepts.
one_line: Missionary Mr. Burch seeks lodging in a village congregation, and Rebecca unexpectedly offers her aunts' brick house.
key_facts: Mr. Burch's mission was to gather funds for the building of his church and keep alive love for the cause in remote neighborhoods.
Mr. Burch offered that he and Mrs. Burch would stay the night and the next day if a member provided entertainment.
Mr. Burch proposed a parlor meeting where his wife and one of his children would wear the native costume and display Syrian handiwork.
The assembly fell silent because members had reasons such as no spare room, a small larder, sickness in the family, or being 'unequally yoked together with unbelievers.'
Mrs. Burch's thin hands fingered her black silk nervously.
Rebecca's heart fluttered with sympathy during the silence.
Mrs. Robinson whispered that the missionaries always used to be entertained at the brick house, and that Rebecca's grandfather never let them sleep anywhere else.
Mrs. Robinson's remark was meant as a stab at Miss Miranda's parsimony, given the four spare chambers closed from January to December.
Rebecca rose and said her aunts, Miss Miranda and Miss Jane Sawyer, would be very happy to have the missionaries visit the brick house.
Rebecca added that the aunts had sent their respects by her.
The aunts would have shuddered at the manner of delivery of their respects.
The audience concluded that Mirandy Sawyer must be making her way uncommonly fast to mansions in the skies.
Mr. Burch bowed courteously and accepted the invitation 'in the same spirit in which it was offered.'
